Datatilsynet fined Ferde AS, a regional toll-road company, NOK 5,000,000 after NRK reported that toll-passage images were sent for manual processing by a contractor with staff in China. The authority found breaches over roughly 12 to 25 months (September 2017 to October 2019): no processor agreement in place for part of that period, no written and dated risk assessment, and no valid transfer mechanism for data going to a third country. The decision is a notice of a fine under Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83, with a right to complain within three weeks.
The French DPA held that a database containing over 6,000,000 fingerprints belonging to suspected or convicted offenders was mismanaged by the Ministry of the Interior.

Between August 2018 and December 2019 Vattenfall Europe Sales GmbH routinely checked customers requesting special bonus contracts for 'switching-prone behaviour', using invoices from earlier contracts, without customers being able to see that this data comparison took place. The Hamburg authority found a breach of the transparency duties in Articles 12 and 13 GDPR, affecting around 500,000 people, and imposed a fine of EUR 901,388.84. The comparison itself was not found unlawful, only the insufficient information. The fine was considerably reduced because Vattenfall cooperated fully and stopped the comparison right after the authority first acted. The decision is final, and a new procedure with transparent information was agreed with the company.

In October 2019 Transavia reported a data breach: an attacker used a password spray / credential stuffing attack to get into its systems, reached an account with very high privileges, and copied data including mailboxes. The AP investigated and found that Transavia had not taken appropriate measures to ensure a security level suited to the risk (for instance lacking multi-factor authentication and not following up on weak password policy compliance). It found a breach of Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It rated the infringement as very serious given the large number of data subjects (over 25 million) and health data, and imposed a fine of EUR 400,000, with a EUR 25,000 increase for negligence offset by a EUR 25,000 reduction for mitigation measures.

The Hungarian DPA issued a reprimand against a controller for the unlawful recording and sharing of a private conversation between two parents and a daycare employee which contained special categories of data.

The Danish tax administration reported a personal data breach after a tax approval letter containing identification, financial and national identification number data was sent by mistake to the wrong recipient. Its initial report said the affected person had been notified before the breach was reported, but a follow-up showed notification only took place about 40 days after the breach became known, on 18 August 2021, which the authority attributed to holiday-period circumstances. Datatilsynet found that the delayed notification did not comply with Article 34(1) GDPR and issued severe criticism (alvorlig kritik), with no fine.

The Icelandic DPA dismissed a complaint from two data subjects regarding the alleged recording of their house and backyard by the video cameras of their neighbors, after the latter demonstrated that the vision field of these cameras were restricted to their own private property.

A data subject complained that Creditinfo, a credit information agency, used a past payment default in its credit scoring. Creditinfo counted the four-year retention period from the date the creditor registered the default, not from the date of the Supreme Court judgment behind the debt, and the complainant had flagged this to Creditinfo. The Authority held that, given fairness, accuracy and proportionality, Creditinfo should have responded to the objection and counted the period from the judgment date, so the processing did not comply with the Act. It ordered Creditinfo to erase the information about the claim from its database and confirm by 22 October 2021.

The Icelandic DPA ruled that the disclosure, by a law firm, of an individual's sensitive personal data is unlawful when the law firm fails to demonstrate that such a disclosure was necessary for the defence of its client's legal claim under Article 9(2)(f) GDPR.

The Danish DPA inspected the dating service Dating.dk ApS in 2018. It found that the company relied on consent but that its single 'click' acceptance of terms and privacy policy was not a valid, unambiguous or explicit consent, and that it processed special category data without a valid Article 9(2) exception. It also found that the company could not show that its risk assessment took account of the risks of processing, including location data and special category data. The DPA issued a reprimand (alvorlig kritik) on these points and an order to bring processing into compliance by 16 November 2021. No fine is imposed in the text.

Datatilsynet inspected whether Falck Danmark A/S, which ran COVID-19 rapid tests on pupils over 12 in Danish primary schools, met its duty to inform data subjects under GDPR Articles 12(1) and 13. Falck made its privacy policy available in print and by QR code at test sites, sent a link by SMS, and relied on the municipalities to pass a link to parents through school platforms, as well as publishing it on its website. Datatilsynet found the information duty was met in this case, but said that making the policy available to pupils alone would not be enough, and recommended child-oriented leaflets or posters. No violation was found and no fine was imposed.

Datatilsynet fined Ultra-Technology AS NOK 125,000 after its managing director ran a credit check on a private individual through the company's credit-rating tool for a purpose outside the business. The authority found no legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR, held the infringement intentional, and treated the later merged company as responsible for the predecessor's processing. It also ordered the company to adopt written routines for credit checks. The proposed fine of NOK 175,000 was reduced because of the length of the proceedings.

An employee complained that a care home had video surveillance cameras, some with audio, recording residents, relatives and staff since 2012, and that staff were watched and evaluated through the footage. The Authority found that the home relied on consent, which cannot be freely given in an employment relationship, and breached the data minimisation principle by filming staff areas such as nurses' stations and kitchens. It also found that the camera system lacked the health-sector documentation required, and that the employee information notice was too general. The Authority issued a reprimand and ordered the kitchen cameras to be refocused on entrances and exits, with footage already collected destroyed, but imposed no fine.

The Greek DPA held that sending bulk emails with all recipients' email addresses entered in the "To" field is not compliant with Article 32 of the GDPR. It recommended the use of BCC as an alternative.

A health clinic employee in a small municipality, while creating letter templates, gained access to image files containing health data of real people with no connection to the municipality, held in the CGM patient system. The municipality reported the incident itself but took no adequate measures for about 11 months beyond asking staff not to open the files. Datatilsynet found a breach of Article 32 in conjunction with Article 24 GDPR, due to fundamental shortcomings in routines for shielding health data and handling deviations. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 400,000 and requested a report on the new routines.

St. Olavs hospital reported three deviations where patient information was stored in shared folders and files accessible to all authenticated users in the Central Norway health region, without access control or logging. The deviations lasted from about two to nine years and included about 21,000 cardiac reports, pulse oximeter reports and plaintext database passwords for substance abuse and child psychiatry clinics. The Norwegian DPA found breaches of security and internal control requirements (Articles 32, 24 and 5) and the Patient Records Act. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 750,000, noting the hospital's corrective measures and self-reporting.

The ICO issued a monetary penalty notice to Your Home Improvements Ltd, a boiler cover seller, for making unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service. The calls were made over June and July 2020, and 1,718 of them went to TPS-registered subscribers. The Commissioner found a serious contravention of regulation 21 of PECR and that the company was negligent, since it failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it. The penalty was £20,000, reduced to £16,000 if paid early.

The Finnish DPA found that the Finnish police had unlawfully relied on the facial recognition software Clearview AI in 2020. It ordered the Finnish Police to bring processing into compliance with the GDPR and to notify identifiable data subjects of this breach.

A patient complained to the Cypriot Commissioner that the Mediterranean Hospital of Cyprus had not fully answered her data access request. The Commissioner asked the hospital for evidence of its position and then issued a formal order with a deadline of 11 March 2021, which the hospital did not meet. The Commissioner found that the hospital had ignored the order and failed to cooperate, breaching Article 31 and Article 58(1)(a) GDPR, and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000. The hospital's later submission of the information in August 2021 was treated as a mitigating factor.

The Danish Data Protection Authority reported Region Syddanmark to the police and recommended a fine of DKK 500,000. A PowerPoint presentation with patient charts, including health data and CPR numbers for 3,915 patients, had been published on the region's website from May 2011. The region's screening tool scanned for CPR numbers but not for the underlying data of PowerPoint files or for health data, so the region had not ensured adequate security. The later update says the city court imposed DKK 1 million, but the High Court acquitted the region on 23 March 2026.

The Italian Garante fined Farpa s.r.l. EUR 1,000 for running a video surveillance system in two residential care homes. Carabinieri found that the cameras were placed differently from the labour inspectorate's authorisation, recorded audio (which the authorisation prohibited), were pointed at beds, and had no adequate notice to guests, relatives or staff. The company argued that the installer was to blame and that the cameras had been switched off; the Garante rejected these points. The decision finds breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 13 and 88 GDPR and Article 114 of the Italian Code, and orders publication of the decision.

A school published on its website a provisional ranking list of teachers who would lose their posts, with asterisks next to names showing who benefited from Law 104/92 (disability/caregiver provisions), and family-needs information, thereby revealing health data of over 50 people. A teacher complained. The school said it was a clerical error and removed the link. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-septies(8) of the Code, fined the school EUR 2,000, and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed since the conduct had ended.

The Danish DPA reported Favrskov Municipality to the police and proposed a fine of DKK 75,000 for insufficient security under Article 32 GDPR. A municipal laptop holding names and personal ID numbers of about 100 people with physical or mental disabilities was stolen in a break-in, and its hard disk was not encrypted and the program had no access logging. The DPA found the failure serious. A later update says the district court (byret) sentenced the municipality to the DKK 75,000 fine.

A property owner complained that an associate of a real estate agency, La Prima S.r.l., contacted her on LinkedIn to offer real estate services for her property, having identified her as the owner from the land registry. The Garante found that using the registry data and the social network for promotion was incompatible with their purposes and had no legal basis (Arts 5, 6, 24, 25 GDPR). For these GDPR violations it issued only a reprimand and an order to adopt measures against promotion without a legal basis, because the case was isolated, the harm minor and the company a micro-enterprise. It imposed a EUR 5,000 fine for a separate violation, namely failing to answer the Garante's repeated information requests (Art. 157 of the Italian Code). A note says the later appeal ended in a final judgment of the Tribunal of Milan described as favourable.

A guest of an institute for the blind in Catania complained that video cameras had been installed in corridors and that visually impaired residents were not informed. The Garante found that, between 10 February and 19 October 2020, cameras filmed the corridor that three visually impaired residents had to use to reach the showers, which breached data minimisation. It also found the privacy notice was missing until June 2020 and afterwards incomplete and not suited to vulnerable people, and that no data protection impact assessment was carried out. The Garante fined the institute EUR 5,000, ordered it to provide the notice also in audio format, and ordered publication of the decision.

A student complained about the university's use of the Respondus proctoring system for online written exams during the COVID-19 emergency, which processed students' biometric data on the basis of consent and involved recordings and behaviour analysis. The Garante found the processing unlawful: no valid legal basis (consent not free), incomplete information, breaches of minimisation, storage limitation and data protection by design, an unlawful transfer of data to the USA, and no adequate DPIA. It imposed a fine, limited the processing of biometric and profiling data, banned transfers to the USA without safeguards and required a report within 30 days. The text states the fine was later reduced by the courts from EUR 200,000 to EUR 150,000.

The Italian DPA investigated Sky Italia after dozens of complaints about unsolicited telemarketing calls for Sky's telephone and internet services. It found that Sky contacted people on lists bought from third parties without checking consent, gave no adequate privacy notice and did not record objections properly. It also found that Sky did not supervise or properly appoint the suppliers and partners who made promotional contacts for it, and ignored objections sent to its official certified e-mail address. The Garante banned further telemarketing based on unchecked third-party lists, ordered Sky to fix its processor appointments and its objection channels, and fined it EUR 3,296,326, with the decision published on the Garante's website.

A complainant reported that the municipality of Montalbano Jonico kept online, in the historical section of its official notice board, a payment determination naming the complainant and his disabled father, including health-related information, birth data, residence, address and details of works and invoices for removing architectural barriers. The municipality said this was a mere error between offices and that it had since redacted the data. The Garante found unlawful dissemination of health data, a breach of data minimisation, and publication beyond the 15-day period without a legal basis. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ceased.

The Directorate of Labour sent a standard email to about 900 addresses in three mass mailings, and by mistake put the recipients in cc instead of bcc, so they could see each other's addresses. A complainant whose email address was shared this way complained to Persónuvernd. The authority found that the disclosure was a security breach that lacked a legal basis, so it breached the GDPR and Act No. 90/2018. It found no duty to notify the breach to the authority, and gave no order because the directorate had already changed its procedures. No fine was imposed.

The CNIL received sixteen complaints about a business directory website that republished SIRENE data, including names and addresses of sole traders, and ignored rectification and erasure requests. An inspection and a formal notice of July 2020 followed, but the company, whose only employee is its president, did not comply. The restricted committee found breaches of Articles 16, 17, 30 and 31 GDPR: it did not rectify or erase data, kept no record of processing, and did not cooperate with the CNIL. It imposed a EUR 3,000 fine and ordered publication of the decision.

A complainant asked the search engine operator to delist online press articles about his political activities that appeared when his name was searched. The request was refused, and the complainant later withdrew his complaint. The Litigation Chamber considered whether to keep examining transparency and information duties (Articles 12, 13 and 14 GDPR) but found the withdrawal left no legal basis for doing so, so it closed the file for technical reasons. No violation was found and no fine or order was imposed. The decision was published with the defendant's direct identifiers removed.

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €56,000 for failing to authenticate a data subject, thereby allowing a fraudulent contracting for multiple new telephone lines. In this regard, Vodafone processed personal data without a legal basis according to Article 6(1) GDPR.

The Catalan DPA issued a reprimand to a city council for creating a WhatsApp group that allowed participants to see the names, phone numbers and profile pictures of other participants, without taking into account the data protection by design principle and without properly providing the information required by Article 13 GDPR.

The ICO issued Saga Personal Finance Limited with a monetary penalty of £75,000 for a serious contravention of regulation 22 of PECR. Between late 2018 and May 2019, marketing emails sent on its behalf by partners and affiliates reached subscribers without valid consent, and the Commissioner found the company instigated them and failed to take reasonable steps to prevent the contravention. The notice says the amount falls to £60,000 if paid early and that an appeal to the First-tier Tribunal is possible.

The UK Information Commissioner issued a monetary penalty notice to Saga Services Limited (SSL) after finding that it instigated unsolicited marketing emails sent by its partners and affiliates without valid consent, contrary to regulation 22 of PECR. The Commissioner found the contravention serious, not deliberate, but negligent, because SSL failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it. The penalty was set at £150,000, with a 20% reduction to £120,000 for payment by 11 October 2021.

The UK Information Commissioner issued a monetary penalty notice to SportsDirect.com Retail Limited under the Data Protection Act 1998 for a serious contravention of regulation 22 of PECR. The company sent about 2.57 million direct marketing emails between 21 December 2019 and 16 February 2020 as part of a 're-engagement campaign' to an aged customer dataset, and could not evidence valid consent or rely on the soft opt-in exemption. The Commissioner found the contravention negligent, not deliberate, and imposed a fine of £70,000, reduced by 20% to £56,000 if paid early.

The ICO issued a monetary penalty notice to We Buy Any Car Limited for sending unsolicited marketing emails and SMS messages to customers. Between April 2019 and April 2020 the company sent about 191.4 million marketing emails and 3.6 million marketing SMS, relying on the 'soft opt-in' without giving customers a simple means to refuse marketing when their details were collected. The Commissioner found a serious contravention of regulation 22 of PECR, found it negligent, and imposed a fine of GBP 200,000, reduced to GBP 160,000 for early payment.

The Hungarian DPA held that the use of a motion-detecting camera to record large areas of a public space in an apartment complex was in breach of the GDPR, because neither the household exemption nor the legitimate interest of the resident who installed the camera could be invoked.

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone Spain €50,000 for unlawfully processing a non-customer's data. Another person had fraudulently entered into a contract with Vodafone and the company failed to take sufficient measures to guarantee their identity.

A former employee of the Austrian Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution and Counterterrorism (BVT) complained that the Ministry of the Interior, via the BVT, had transmitted his unredacted personnel-related files, classified 'Vertraulich', to the parliamentary BVT investigation committee. The Data Protection Authority upheld the complaint. It found that the unredacted transmission breached the right to secrecy under section 1 DSG, to the extent it concerned his work as a source protected under Art. 53(3) last sentence B-VG, and that it also infringed the GDPR principles of fairness/transparency and data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(a) and (c)). No fine is mentioned in the text.

Region Midtjylland, a Danish regional health authority, notified a personal data breach in June 2020. Patient records (up to 100,000 paper files with health data and CPR numbers) were kept in a building at Livstilscenter Brædstrup, where keycards gave access to all three buildings and windows were not frosted, so patients and staff, and passers-by, could see or enter. Datatilsynet found the physical security measures inadequate and reported the region to the police, proposing a fine of DKK 400,000. The city court (byret) imposed a fine of DKK 300,000.

The DPC announced that Vodafone Ireland Limited pleaded guilty in the Dublin Metropolitan District Court to seven charges of sending unsolicited marketing texts, emails and calls without consent. The cases arose from customers who had opted out or stated they did not want marketing, but whose requests were not recorded because agents did not follow proper procedures. The court imposed fines totalling EUR 1,400. The text is a press release covering two companies; this entry covers only the Vodafone part.

Twelve former shareholders of OASTH (the Thessaloniki urban transport organisation) complained that its president named them at a press conference and in a press release listing 29 former shareholders, with their stakes, purchase prices and contract dates. They also complained that their access/objection requests went unanswered. The Authority found that publishing the names of two shareholders, who had made no claims, breached Articles 4 and 5 of Law 2472/1997, and that failing to answer the requests breached Articles 12 and 13 of that law. It fined OASTH EUR 3,000 and EUR 7,000 (EUR 10,000 in total) and warned it to comply with the GDPR going forward. The case was decided under the old Law 2472/1997, not the GDPR.

A law firm, acting for a complainant, asked an insurance company for access to surveillance material (observation reports, photos and videos) the company had gathered about him while pursuing an injury-related compensation claim. The insurer refused, citing Section 22 of the Danish Data Protection Act and its interest in defending a possible lawsuit and in police investigation of suspected fraud. The Danish DPA found the refusal unjustified because no overriding interest was shown, and issued a serious criticism for breach of Article 15 GDPR read with Section 22 of the Act. The material was handed over in January 2021, which the DPA noted but did not change the outcome. No fine was imposed, and the DPA did not rule on the lawfulness of the surveillance itself.

A former employee of a municipal transport company complained that, after his dismissal, his employment certificate stated he was dismissed for a criminal offence, and that the company never answered his request for a copy of the bus CCTV footage he needed for his defence. The Authority found a breach of the data minimisation principle and of the right of access and response-deadline rules. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 for the access breach and EUR 3,000 for the minimisation breach, EUR 8,000 in total.

A complaint was lodged by a lawyer for a former municipal employee about a municipality's collection and use of his personal data. The municipality obtained information about him by phone from a public body where he had previously worked, and used it in deciding to dismiss him and to reject his application for another post. The DPA held that the data collection and use was necessary for public-authority decisions and was lawful under the previous Act 77/2000 (for the 2018 dismissal) and Act 90/2018 (for the later job application). It found that the processing complied with the data protection principles and the complaint was not upheld. Consent was rejected as a basis because of the employment relationship.

The Spanish DPA concluded that it is not justifiable to generally deny access to video recordings showing third parties, because new technologies allow to anonymize images in a way that third parties are no longer harmed.

The Icelandic DPA held that a school infringed the parents of a student's Articles 12 and 15 GDPR rights for failing to provide them with emails they were entitled to receive and withholding data without adequate notice. However, it was found to be entitled to withhold emails with other parents as providing such data would adversely affect their rights and interests.

The Norwegian Data Protection Authority, on its own initiative, asked the Directorate of the Norwegian Correctional Service in December 2020 for its register of processing activities and a description of who is responsible for processing within the service. The Directorate had no central overview; it had only a draft listing ten processing activities. The Authority found this to be a deviation from the GDPR's record-keeping requirement in Article 30 and issued three binding orders: establish a full overview of processing, document how processing responsibility is allocated, and submit the internal control documentation. No fine was imposed.

A customer returned a product bought in instalments on his credit card and found the instalments kept being charged. He asked Kotsovolos for the company's request to the bank, but the company refused, calling it internal communication. He also complained about the issuing bank, National Bank of Greece, which did not answer his access request. The Authority found that both breached the right of access under Article 15(1) with Article 12(1)-(3) GDPR. Kotsovolos satisfied the request only after months and after the Authority intervened. It fined each of the two companies EUR 20,000.

A customer returned a product bought by card instalments and complained to the Authority about two parties: the retailer Kotsovolos and the issuing bank, National Bank of Greece. He said neither satisfied his access request about the retailer's request to release the instalments. The Authority found that the Bank gave no answer, even a negative one, and did not meet the access request, breaching Articles 15(1) and 12(1)-(3) GDPR. It fined the Bank EUR 20,000 and also fined the retailer EUR 20,000 for the same articles.

A doctor complained that an online doctor directory and appointment-booking company ignored her repeated requests to delete her data from its platform. The company did not answer her, a medical association, or the Authority, and the data was only removed about 18 months later, after the Authority summoned the company. The complainant withdrew her complaint, but the Authority continued ex officio and found breaches of lawfulness, storage limitation, accountability, ease of exercising rights and erasure. It ordered the company to bring its processing into compliance and set up measures within one month, and fined it EUR 5,000.
The Spanish DPA fined a marketing company €15,000 for sending automated advertising emails without consent, even after a complainant exercised their right to erasure.

A complainant reported that the bank's automated phone line gave out the details of recent Affinity Card transactions when the caller only entered a national ID number (DNI), with no further identity check. The AEPD opened a sanctioning procedure for a presumed breach of Article 32 GDPR and proposed a fine of EUR 200,000. The bank paid EUR 120,000 on 18 August 2021, using both the 20% reduction for admitting responsibility and the 20% reduction for voluntary payment, and the AEPD declared the procedure terminated.

Following a complaint, ANSPDCP investigated Actamedica SRL after a courier parcel containing a person's biological samples and money was lost or damaged. The authority found insufficient security measures, failure to notify the breach to the authority, and failure to answer the data subject's access request. It imposed two fines totalling the equivalent of EUR 3,000 and a warning for the access and response failures, plus two corrective orders.

The UK Information Commissioner issued a monetary penalty notice to DialADeal Scotland Ltd, a company that made unsolicited direct marketing calls, many of them about non-existent 'Green Deal' energy schemes, using spoofed caller IDs and generic trading names. Between 11 August 2019 and 12 March 2020 the company made 558,250 calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service without consent, and it failed to identify itself as required. The Commissioner found the contraventions of Regulations 21 and 24 of PECR to be serious and deliberate, and alternatively negligent, and imposed a penalty of £150,000, reducible by 20% for early payment.
The Slovak DPA issued an Opinion condemning a Slovak-US tax information exchange Agreement, related to the implementation of FATCA, for not complying with the GDPR data transfer requirements.
The Spanish DPA fined a logistics company €1,800 for sending an individual unsolicited commercial communications after they had exercised their right to object.

The Irish DPC ran an own-volition inquiry into whether WhatsApp Ireland met its GDPR transparency duties towards users and non-users, including how it explains its sharing of data with other Facebook companies. The decision found infringements of Articles 5(1)(a), 12, 13 and 14. The DPC's draft decision proposed a much lower fine. The EDPB then resolved the dispute under Article 65 and instructed the DPC to reassess and increase the fine. The DPC imposed a reprimand, an order to bring processing into compliance within 3 months, and a total administrative fine of EUR 225 million. WhatsApp's arguments that its lack of prior infringements and its good faith efforts should be mitigating factors were rejected as neutral.

The DPC opened an own-volition inquiry after MOVE Ireland reported the loss of SD memory cards holding recordings of domestic-violence group sessions, with participants' disclosures about partners and family. MOVE could not locate 18 of its 44 cards. The Commissioner found that MOVE failed to implement appropriate security measures under Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) GDPR, and imposed a reprimand, an order to bring processing into compliance, and an administrative fine of EUR 1,500. The fine is calculated on Article 5(1)(f) alone.

The Spanish DPA fined a controller acting on behalf of Vodafone €20,000 for making unsolicited commercial calls to a data subject. The controller failed to adequately check phone numbers against a list of users who did not wish to receive calls.

The Norwegian DPA instructed Google to delete a search result about a data subject's criminal past, but agreed with their decision to refuse erasure for two other search results. The DPA agreed these were still relevant after 10 years, in part because the data subject was a CSO in a company planning to go public, and the information was deemed to be of public interest. The Privacy Appeals Board later upheld the DPA's decision.

The Danish Data Protection Authority reported the Danish Immigration Agency to the police and recommended a fine of DKK 150,000. The Authority found that the agency had not met the GDPR requirements for an appropriate level of security in its processing of residents' records at two departure centres. The agency had no procedures for systematically using its event logs, had not assessed risks to data subjects in the SALTO system, and had not made adequate backups, so some data was lost in a June 2020 incident. The text adds that the case was settled on 18 March 2024 with a fine notice of DKK 150,000.

Two complaints by one individual alleged that the address publisher N*** AG obtained consent for passing his address data to third parties for marketing, through a pre-ticked checkbox on the storage-compartment contract form (2018 and 2019). The authority found that the box was an objection (opt-out) under Art. 21 GDPR, not a consent, and that no data was passed on for third-party marketing because he had objected. The complaints were dismissed and the decision is final.
The UK DPA fined a direct marketing company approximately €58,600 (£50,000) for making illegal marketing calls to people about their pensions.

The Norwegian DPA fined Waxing Palace AS NOK 100,000. The company runs a waxing salon and had camera surveillance covering its reception area. After investigating a complaint, the authority found that the company had no legal basis for the surveillance and did not give good enough information about it. The authority considered the case serious because the surveillance affected both employees and customers, and customers see a waxing salon visit as a private errand. The company could appeal until 20 August 2021.

A data subject complained that a Budapest district mayor's office had displayed and published his name and home address during an online public hearing, in the live stream, the video recording and the minutes, and had refused his request for erasure. The Authority found that the disclosure breached Article 6(1) and Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, that the refusal of erasure under Article 17(1)(d) was unlawful, and that the information given before the hearing did not meet Article 12. It issued a reprimand and ordered the office to act on the erasure request for the identifying data, but imposed no fine, finding the reprimand and order sufficient and proportionate.
The Spanish DPA fined a gymnastics club €5,000 for posting images of two children on its Instagram page, despite the express denial of consent by their mother.

A complainant asked a staffing agency to erase his personal data after it sent him unsolicited job offers by SMS, using contact details it took from his public job advertisement on the AMS job portal. The agency did not respond to the erasure request and did not answer the authority's requests in substance, relying only on having received the data from the AMS. The authority found that the agency breached the transparency principle and Article 14 by not informing the data subject when collecting the data, so the data was unlawfully processed from the start and the right to erasure was violated. It ordered the agency to erase all the complainant's data within four weeks.

A data subject complained that Creditinfo Lánstraust entered his debt payment record on its default register without giving him prior notice, and that Creditinfo refused to erase the effect of that entry on credit reports. Creditinfo said it sent a notice to his registered address on 16 March 2020 and that the letter was never returned, and it confirmed the printing and posting through its mail provider. Persónuvernd could not resolve the factual dispute over receipt, but found the notice procedure adequate under the GDPR and the licence terms. It held that the processing complied with the law and that no erasure was required, while noting that under a new licence from May 2021 such effects should now be gone.

A housing company told residents in a March 2020 notice that a resident who tested positive for coronavirus had to report this to the property manager. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that collecting such health data needs a lawful basis under Articles 6 and 9 GDPR and compliance with data minimisation and data protection by design, and that the controller had not assessed these. Because the controller said no personal data had actually been collected, the Deputy Ombudsman issued a warning under Article 58(2)(a) instead of using other corrective powers.

A customer complained that an insurer's employee had twice emailed health-related information and medical forms to wrong email addresses. The CNPD opened an investigation, inspected the premises in July 2019 and found failures on email security, breach documentation, breach notification, communication to the data subject and DPO contact details. The restricted formation imposed a fine of EUR 135,000 based on Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1)(a) and (b) and 33(5) GDPR. It did not base the fine on the Article 33(1), 34(1) and 37(7) breaches, though it found them. It also ordered the insurer to secure emails containing special-category data within two months. The investigation head had proposed EUR 275,000.

A private individual, in a long-running neighbour dispute, emailed a municipality's department where the data subject worked as a kindergarten teacher. The email attached an unredacted medical expert opinion about her health, which he had obtained in civil court proceedings. The authority found that he processed health data without a legal basis under Art. 9 GDPR and that he acted intentionally, for personal motives. It imposed a fine of EUR 600 plus EUR 60 in procedure costs, and the decision is final.

The Romanian DPA fined a natural person approximately €200 (RON 985.5) for disclosing copies of a pay slip and a kindergarten register containing personal data on their personal Facebook page and via flyers they distributed, in in violation of Articles 5, 6 and 14 GDPR.
The Spanish DPA fined the owner of a dating website €2000 for publishing contact data without the consent of the data subject.

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €120,000 (reduced to €96,000) for processing personal data without a legal basis, since they did not prevent a third party from fraudulently using someone's personal data to contract its service, and for not complying with the right to erasure.

The Belgian DPA closed a case regarding the use of a municipality database for a political campaign, despite finding a violation of the purpose limitation principle. The case involved two defendants, and it could not be established that the first defendant had used the database for the campaign. The second defendant, who did have access to the database, died after the complaint.

The UK DPA fined a controller approximately €200,000 (£170,000) for contacting almost 200,000 individuals who had registered their intent not to receive marketing calls with the Telephone Preference Service ('TPS'). In particular, the controller had failed to check datasets purchased from 11 third-party data providers against the TPS.

The Spanish DPA fined a controller €60,000 for failing to respond to an access request, and for processing personal data without a legal basis, since it could not prove it had entered into a contract with the data subject.

The CNIL restricted committee fined the US company designated 'X' EUR 400,000 for failing to inform data subjects (Art. 14 GDPR) and for having no legal act governing the processing done for it by a lobbying firm (Art. 28 GDPR). The lobbying firm had compiled a file of 201 people resident in France, with contact details, influence scores and comments, during the campaign for the renewal of the EU approval of glyphosate. The committee also ordered publication of the decision, which will stop naming the company after two years.

The AEPD investigated Mercadona's facial recognition system in its stores, which was meant to detect people with final convictions and restraining orders against the company or its staff. It found that the processing of special-category biometric data was prohibited and lacked a legal basis, that information to data subjects was inadequate, that data minimisation and data protection by design were breached, and that the impact assessment was deficient. A fine of EUR 2,000,000 + 100,000 + 500,000 + 500,000 + 50,000 = EUR 3,150,000 was proposed. Mercadona paid voluntarily with a 20% reduction (EUR 2,520,000), which ended the procedure. The AEPD also prohibited all facial recognition processing in its stores.

After an ex officio investigation and an on-site inspection in June 2019, the Italian DPA examined how Deliveroo Italy processes the personal data of its roughly 8,000 riders through a platform run centrally by the UK parent. It found breaches of the processing principles, transparency, safeguards for automated decision-making and profiling, privacy by design, records of processing, security, impact assessment, DPO notification and the employment-context and remote-monitoring rules. It ordered the company to bring its processing into compliance within set deadlines and imposed a fine of EUR 2,500,000, with publication of the order.

The Lombardy Region published on its institutional website lists of students applying for school grants (textbooks, technology, scholarships) for families with an ISEE of up to about EUR 15,000. The lists showed names, school and class in clear for tens of thousands of people, including applicants who received no grant. The Garante held that the data could reveal economic hardship, that publication had no adequate legal basis and breached data minimisation. The Region had removed the data, so no further corrective measures were ordered, but a fine of EUR 200,000 was imposed and the decision was ordered to be published.

Following a report, the Garante investigated the new parking meters in Rome, which require drivers to enter the vehicle plate. It found that Roma Capitale, as controller, gave no adequate privacy notice, had not appointed ATAC and Flowbird as processors under Article 28, had set no retention periods (8.6 million parking records were stored), and used weak security (unencrypted http transfers, plaintext short passwords, no access logs, MD5 hashing of old plates). The Garante found violations of Articles 5, 12, 13, 25, 28 and 32 GDPR, fined Roma Capitale EUR 800,000, ordered corrective security measures within 30 days and ordered publication of the decision.

Atac, the Rome public transport company, processed licence-plate and payment data from new parking meters on behalf of Roma Capitale without having been formally appointed as processor under Article 28 GDPR. It also had no record of processing activities and weak security: unencrypted http traffic, plain-text 5-character passwords and no activity logs. About 8.6 million parking records were involved. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5, 6, 30 and 32, fined Atac EUR 400,000, ordered it to add application logs and security for stored data within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

The CNIL's restricted committee fined the insurance company (called X in the published text, part of a group called Y) after an on-site inspection in October 2019. The company kept customer and prospect data in its active systems for longer than its own retention schedule or the legal limits allowed, and its information notices for telephone prospecting did not meet Articles 13 and 14 GDPR at the time of the inspection. The committee imposed an administrative fine of EUR 1,750,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but dropped the proposed compliance injunction because the company had by then brought its practices into line on those points.

A complainant repeatedly objected to promotional emails from a used-car company and sent STOP replies in 2019 and 2020, but the emails continued. The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber first issued a 'light' decision (12/2020) ordering compliance within one month, which the company did not follow. It then decided the case on the merits without the company's submissions. It found breaches of the right to object and the right to erasure, combined with the duty to respond within one month, and issued a reprimand with orders to honour the objection and erase the data, notify recipients under Article 19, and report back to the DPA. No fine was imposed.

The Danish DPA reported Region Syddanmark to the police and recommended DKK 500,000. On 23 March 2026 the Western High Court (Vestre Landsret) fined the region DKK 500,000 in this case. The district court (Retten i Kolding) had fined the region DKK 1 million in total for this case and a second one, on 23 December 2024; the High Court acquitted it in the second. In Denmark the data protection authority cannot fine: it reports the case to the police and recommends an amount, and a court sets the fine.

On 15 July 2021 the Luxembourg data protection authority (CNPD) fined Amazon Europe Core S.à r.l. EUR 746,000,000 and ordered it to change its practices on pain of EUR 746,000 a day, over its processing of personal data for interest-based advertising. The Tribunal administratif upheld the decision on 18 March 2025; its release names Articles 6, 12 to 17 and 21 GDPR (lawful basis, transparency, access, rectification, erasure and objection). On 12 March 2026 the Cour administrative annulled the decision in full. It confirmed most of the infringements found when the investigation opened, which are now remedied, but held that the CNPD had not assessed fault (intent or negligence) and had not properly weighed which of the available measures was most suitable (it had imposed a fine almost automatically), and sent the case back to the CNPD to do both. It found Article 21 outside the scope of the CNPD's investigation. The CNPD says the court endorsed its approach almost entirely and that the fine was annulled because of later case law of the Court of Justice. Fino has found no new decision.

A court probation officer lost an unencrypted USB stick holding personal data of 400 people under supervision, including health data and data on criminal convictions. The court president reported the breach, and the authority opened proceedings of its own initiative. It found that the court had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures for portable storage, having left the securing of the stick to the officer. It imposed an administrative fine of PLN 10,000 on the court president, taking into account the cap for public-sector bodies and the good cooperation of the controller.

The EDPB adopted an urgent binding decision under Article 66 GDPR. Following a provisional measure taken by the Hamburg DPA against WhatsApp, the EDPB analysed WhatsApp's data sharing practices with Facebook. The EDPB did not confirm the provisional measure, but given the high likelihood that data sharing is taking place, it requested the Irish DPA to investigate certain key blind spots in WhatsApp's data processing, including whether data is actually shared with Facebook, whether Facebook acts as processor or joint controller, and whether the legal basis identified in the privacy policy is adequate in relation to the actual processing.

The Danish DPA reported Medicals Nordic I/S, a provider of COVID-19 tests, to the police and recommended a fine of DKK 600,000. The company sent citizens' confidential and health data, including personal ID numbers, via WhatsApp groups that staff without a work need, including former employees, could read. The district court (byret) imposed a fine of DKK 400,000, and the company has appealed seeking acquittal.
The Spanish DPA fined a bank €50,000 for sending commercial communications on the envelope of a letter to a client that had exercised their right to object.

A customer who had a dispute with an Amazon seller complained that the seller, Malagatrom, S.L.U., had published her name, address, mobile number, and her husband's name and mobile number in a public seller-feedback comment, after threatening to do so in a reply. The inspection found the complaint true and also found three other comments in which the company disclosed customers' personal data. The AEPD held that publishing the data on a public website had no lawful basis under Article 6 GDPR, and that the related confidentiality breach was absorbed into that single infringement. It fined the company EUR 4,000 and ordered it to remove the comments and prevent similar conduct within one month.

A father complained that his child's paediatrician refused to give him access to the child's medical file, including tax receipts for the examinations, and would not give him her email address. The Authority held that a parent exercising parental care has the right of access under Article 15 GDPR, and that the doctor failed to facilitate it, only offering collection from her lawyer's office in another city during Covid restrictions. It found breaches of Articles 15(1) and 12(1),(2) and fined the doctor EUR 5,000.

The Spanish DPA fined Telefonica €75,000 (reduced to €45,000) for processing personal data without a legal basis. Telefonica had continued to call a data subject for direct marketing purposes after they had exercised their right to object.

A private company, Nordbornholms Byggeforretning ApS, disclosed to two of its customers that a former employee had committed and admitted criminal fraud, including details of the alleged offence. Following a citizen's complaint in 2018, the Danish Data Protection Authority reported the company to the police and proposed a fine of DKK 400,000. The district court (byretten) imposed a fine of DKK 100,000.

A citizen complained that the Danish Business Authority recorded his telephone call without consent. The authority had recorded all incoming calls to its customer centre since 1 June 2018, mainly to document threats for police reports and for training and quality purposes. The Danish Data Protection Agency, after consulting its Data Council, found that the general practice of recording all calls could not rest on Article 6(1)(e) and that recording for quality and training purposes required consent under Article 6(1)(a). It issued serious criticism for non-compliance with Article 6(1) and recommended that the authority report within 4 weeks how it would bring the practice into line. No fine was imposed.

The Croatian DPA fined an IT company for failing to take appropriate security measures for the processing of personal data. The inadequate level of technical security resulted in a security breach on data controller's IT system, whereby hackers were able to process the personal data of 28,085 data subjects.

Mermaids, a UK charity supporting transgender and gender non-conforming children and young people, left an internal email group on an online service with default public settings. Around 780 pages of emails with the personal data of 550 people, including children and some health and sex-life data, could be found through search engines from 25 May 2018 to 14 June 2019. A newspaper journalist alerted a service user, and the charity then secured the group and reported itself to the ICO. The ICO found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) and (2) GDPR and imposed a fine of £25,000. It treated the breaches as negligent rather than deliberate, and took account of the charity's prompt remedial action, its cooperation and its income.
The DPA fined Jamk University of Applied Sciences €25,000 for unnecessarily processing the location data of its employees. The DPA also imposed a ban on the processing of location data.

The Spanish DPA fined an individual €1500 for sharing personal data related to the sex life of the complainant on a website. The DPA rejected the individual's claim that a BDSM submission contract is a valid form of consent, and a legitimate basis for the publishing of such personal data.

The AEPD fined an individual EUR 1,000 for using a third party's personal data to apply for a micro-loan through an online lending portal, without any legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. The complaint came from a court that had convicted the individual of minor fraud linked to that loan application. The individual did not respond to the opening agreement, so the proceeding went straight to a decision. The AEPD treated the conduct as intentional, which it counted as an aggravating factor.

A private individual shared on Twitter a video showing a man assaulting a woman while her young son tried to intervene. The faces of the woman and the child were not pixelated. The AEPD opened its own investigation and a sanction procedure for processing personal data (images) without a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR, proposing a EUR 10,000 fine. The respondent paid EUR 6,000 within the deadline, using both 20% reductions (acknowledging responsibility and voluntary payment). The AEPD therefore declared the procedure terminated under Article 85 LPACAP.

The Polish DPA fined a foundation approximately €3,000 (PLN 13,644) for failing to inform both the DPA and data subjects of a data breach. The DPA also ordered the foundation to communicate the personal data breach to the data subjects.

The Spanish DPA warned a Spanish city council for infringing Article 30 GDPR by not maintaining a record of its processing activities, and Article 31 of the Spanish Data Protection Act by not making a record of its processing activities available by electronic means.

The Luxembourg data protection authority opened an own-initiative investigation into a group of companies, focusing on video surveillance, and visited the premises of Société A (a bakery and pastry manufacturer) in March 2019. It found that a camera covered part of the public road and that ten cameras permanently filmed employees at their workstations, breaching data minimisation. It also found that employees and third parties (customers, suppliers, visitors) were not given the information required by Article 13 GDPR. The restricted formation fined the company EUR 12,500 for both breaches (the head of investigation had proposed EUR 17,000) and ordered it to bring its information to employees and third parties into line with Article 13 within two months. It declined to issue the proposed corrective measure on data minimisation because of the compliance steps already taken.

The ICO issued a monetary penalty notice to Brazier Consulting Services Limited, a claims management firm, for making unsolicited direct marketing calls about claims management services without the subscribers' consent, in breach of regulation 21A of PECR. The calls were made between February and July 2019, and the ICO counted 11,489,873 marketing calls that led to 316 complaints. The ICO found the contravention serious and negligent, and imposed a penalty of £200,000, reducible to £160,000 for early payment.

The Finnish DPA found that a controller (X) and a processor (Y) had failed to enter into a data processing agreement pursuant to Article 28(3) GDPR. It decided not to impose a fine firstly because the data processing operations had already ended, and secondly due to the very low turnover of Y and the fact that it had already filed for bankruptcy.

The Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board rejected a complaint where a data subject asked the DPA to require Microsoft to uncover the identity (via IP addresses used at login) of alleged hackers of their Hotmail account.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a controller €10,000 for issuing an invoice containing incorrect data in violation of the accuracy principle.

The UK Information Commissioner issued an enforcement notice to Emailmovers Limited, a marketing data company. EML described itself as a processor, but the Commissioner found it was a controller for business-to-consumer data it licensed and sold. The Commissioner found that EML had not identified a lawful basis or given transparent notice, so it breached the fairness, lawfulness and transparency principle in Article 5(1)(a) UK GDPR. The notice requires EML, within three months, to notify data subjects, stop processing data without a compliant notice or valid consent, and keep consent records. No fine was imposed.
The Lithuanian DPA fined a sports club approximately €20,000 for processing the biometric data of its customers and employees in violation of Articles 9(1), 13(1) and (2), 30, and 35(1) GDPR.

IMY investigated Stockholm's public transport operator SL after media reported it would equip ticket inspectors with body-worn cameras recording image and sound. IMY found that SL's pre-recording technique (continuous recording stored for at least one minute) lacked a legal basis and breached data minimisation, that recording to establish the identity of passengers given a surcharge was unlawful and excessive, and that SL gave passengers insufficient information. Actual recording during ongoing threats was found lawful. IMY imposed a total administrative fine of SEK 16 million, split SEK 4 million, 8 million and 4 million for the three infringements.

A personal data breach at an insurance agent (acting as processor) sent an insurance offer and calculation containing a client's PESEL number, name, place, postcode and insurance details to the wrong recipient. The insurer, the controller, did not notify the supervisory authority or the data subject. The Polish DPA found breaches of Article 33(1) and Article 34(1) GDPR, imposed an administrative fine of PLN 159,176 (stated as about EUR 35,000), and ordered the insurer to notify the data subject within 3 days. The decision is marked final (prawomocna).

A person who was not a Magyar Telekom customer kept receiving unsolicited newsletters because a customer had mistakenly given the person's Gmail address. Repeated erasure requests were answered with unsubscribe links that led to a login page, which the complainant could not use. The Authority rejected the request to order erasure as moot, since the address had been deleted during the procedure. It found ex officio breaches of Articles 5(1)(d), 6(1), 12 and 17, plus a general practice infringing Articles 12(2) and 25(2). It ordered Telekom to change its practice so that exercising data subject rights does not require unnecessary extra conditions, and fined it HUF 10,000,000.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined an energy company €12,000 for making marketing calls to a data subject that had signed up to a Robinson List.

The Danish Data Protection Agency reported Vejle Municipality to the police for a fine after the municipality notified a personal data breach. The municipal dental service had a standing practice of automatically sending welcome letters with both parents' addresses to both holders of parental responsibility, without checking whether the address could be disclosed, so parents received the other parent's (and the child's) address even where that parent had address protection. The authority found the municipality had not implemented appropriate security measures. The district court imposed DKK 50,000 and the high court increased it to DKK 100,000.

The Information Commissioner’s Office fined a home improvement company approximately €153,000 (£130,000) for making more than 900,000 direct marketing calls from numbers that masked the company's identity, and that were in part directed at individuals who had opted-out.

Huppuís ehf., which runs an ice cream shop, filmed a staff area with CCTV where young employees changed clothes. A complaint was lodged in November 2018 that the monitoring was not signposted, that staff were not informed, and that they had no proper changing space. The Icelandic authority found the monitoring had no adequate legal basis, lacked transparency and proportionality, and that staff were not informed. It imposed a fine of ISK 5,000,000, ordered the monitoring of the back area to stop and the footage to be deleted, and ordered updated procedures and staff information.

A complainant, the director of a care association, complained that an audit report sent by the agency to union representatives and a social conciliator contained his salary and details of a company he managed, and that the agency answered his access request late. The Chambre contentieuse found that the late reply to the access request breached Article 15(1) read with Articles 12(3) and 13(1)(c). It also found that sending the report to the union representatives and the conciliator breached Article 6(1)(e), because that disclosure was not necessary for the agency's public task. As the agency is a public authority, no fine could be imposed, so a reprimand was issued and the rest of the complaint was dismissed.

A buyer paid a deposit on a flat to a real estate company and received no data protection information. The company's reply to the AEPD cited the repealed Organic Law 15/1999 and did not meet the Article 13 GDPR information duties. The AEPD opened a penalty procedure proposing a EUR 2,000 fine. The company paid EUR 1,200 on 9 June 2021, using both 20% reductions for voluntary payment and acknowledging responsibility. The AEPD therefore declared the procedure terminated under Article 85 of the LPACAP.

Following an on-site inspection in November 2018 and online checks in 2020 and 2021, the CNIL restricted committee sanctioned an online private-sales company (name redacted) that operates in France, Spain, Italy and Portugal. The company was found in breach of the storage-limitation principle, the duty to inform data subjects, the rights of erasure and the security obligation under the GDPR, as well as French data protection law (Art. 82) and the ePrivacy rules on electronic prospecting (Art. L. 34-5 CPCE). The committee imposed an administrative fine of EUR 500,000 (EUR 300,000 for the GDPR breaches and EUR 200,000 for the others), ordered compliance with a EUR 500 per day penalty, and ordered publication of the decision.

The ICO issued a monetary penalty notice to Global One 2015, a charity, after it was found to have instigated around 573,000 unsolicited marketing text messages sent in April and May 2020 through a third-party supplier. The Commissioner found that Global One had no valid consent for the messages, relying instead on indirect consent, and that its opt-out arrangements were ineffective, breaching regulations 22 and 23 of PECR. The penalty was set at £10,000, reduced to £8,000 if paid early.

The ICO found that Papa John's (GB) Limited sent 168,022 direct marketing text messages between October 2019 and April 2020 to customers who had ordered by telephone. The company had not offered those customers a simple way to refuse marketing when their details were collected, so it could not rely on the soft opt-in exemption. The Commissioner found a serious contravention of regulation 22 of PECR and found it negligent, not deliberate, and imposed a monetary penalty of £10,000, reduced to £8,000 if paid early.

The CNPD opened an investigation into a company's video surveillance and vehicle geolocation systems and visited its premises in March 2019. It found that cameras permanently watched the reception workstation and the staff entrance and smoking area, that the information given to employees and third parties was incomplete, and that the geolocation software lacked individual access accounts and a proper retention limit. The restricted formation found breaches of Articles 5(1)(c), 5(1)(e), 13 and 32(1) GDPR and imposed a single fine of EUR 7,200. It also ordered the company to bring its Article 13 information into compliance within two months. No corrective measure was ordered on the geolocation system because that processing had been stopped.

The CNPD opened an investigation into a car dealership group's video surveillance and geolocation and, after an on-site visit in December 2018, focused on Société A. It found that two of its thirty cameras filmed the public road and six cameras permanently monitored employees at their workstations, breaching data minimisation. It also found that employees and third parties (customers, suppliers, visitors) were not properly informed under Article 13. The restricted formation fined the company EUR 7,600 and ordered it to bring its information notices into compliance within two months.

The CNPD ran a thematic audit campaign on the role of data protection officers and opened an audit of a transport company in September 2018. The investigator found that the DPO was not systematically involved in data protection matters, that his autonomy was not guaranteed, and that his monitoring and advisory tasks were not formally carried out. The restricted committee upheld the breaches of Articles 38(1), 38(3), 39(1)(a) and 39(1)(b) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000. It also ordered the company to comply with each of these articles within four months.

The Italian DPA inspected Foodinho s.r.l. (Glovo group delivery platform) in July 2019 on its own initiative, looking at how it processes data of its riders through the platform and algorithms. It found unlawful processing breaching the general principles (lawfulness, fairness, minimisation, storage limitation), information duties, safeguards for automated decision-making and profiling, privacy by design and default, records of processing, security, DPIA, DPO notification, and the employment-law rules on remote monitoring. It ordered the company to bring its processing into line within 60 days (with algorithm and feedback checks to start within 60 days and finish within 90 more). It also imposed a fine of EUR 2,600,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A patient complained that a dentist made him fill in a medical questionnaire asking about infectious diseases including HIV, and then declined to treat him after he disclosed being HIV-positive. The Garante found that the HIV information was collected without a concrete treatment purpose, since care was in fact refused, so the legal basis for processing health data fell away. It found a breach of the Article 5 principles and fined the dentist EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

Following an inspection campaign on whistleblowing applications, the Garante examined the Bologna airport operator's use of the 'WB Confidential' platform supplied by a processor. The platform ran over unencrypted http, stored data unencrypted, and navigation logs on the whistleblowing site were kept without safeguards. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 25, 32 and 35 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 40,000 for the breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 25 and 32, imposed no fine for the missing DPIA given the early application period, ordered no corrective measures because the conduct had ceased, and ordered publication.

During a round of inspections of whistleblowing software, the Garante checked the 'WB Confidential' application that aiComply supplies as a processor to Bologna airport operator AdB. It found that aiComply used two other companies for system and application maintenance without any contract or authorisation as sub-processors. It also found the application ran over plain http, kept data in the database unencrypted, and had a System Administrator account shared by two people. The Garante held that this breached Articles 28 and 32 GDPR and fined aiComply EUR 20,000. It ordered the company to bring its processing into compliance and report back within 30 days, and it ordered publication of the decision.

A data subject asked a company on 14 November 2020 for access to his personal data and for the source of his data-box address. The company never replied, even after the Office warned it in February 2021 and issued a repeated request in March 2021. The Office found a breach of the right of access under Article 15(1) GDPR and imposed a fine of CZK 50,000 by penalty order.

A data subject asked a company on 12 November 2020 for access to his personal data and the source of his data-box address, and received no reply. The Czech DPA warned the company in February 2021 and again in March 2021, and it still did not respond. The DPA issued a penalty order finding a breach of the right of access under Article 15(1) GDPR and fined the company CZK 50,000. The aggravating factor was that the company did not remedy the breach even after repeated warnings.

A data subject asked a company on 14 November 2020 for access to his personal data and for the source of his data box address. The company never replied, even after the DPA warned it on 15 February 2021 and sent a repeated call on 25 March 2021. The DPA found a breach of the right of access under Article 15(1) GDPR (and Article 12 duties) and issued a penalty order imposing a fine of CZK 50,000. The failure to remedy after repeated warnings was treated as aggravating.

A data subject asked a company on 12 November 2020 for access to the personal data it held and the source of his data-box address, and received no reply. The Czech DPA warned the company in February 2021 and again in March 2021, but it still did not respond. The Office found a breach of the right of access under Article 15(1) GDPR and imposed a fine of CZK 50,000 by summary order. The failure to remedy after repeated warnings was treated as aggravating.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in May 2021 into Dreamtime Call S.R.L., which had been accused in a complaint of repeatedly phoning an individual without prior consent. The company confirmed receiving the authority's information requests but never answered them. It was fined RON 9,852.2 (about EUR 2,000) as a misdemeanour for failing to supply the requested information. It was also ordered to send all the requested information within 5 working days of receiving the minutes.

IMY investigated, after a complaint, the round-the-clock real-time camera surveillance of the vehicle halls at eight fire stations run by the Östra Skaraborg Rescue Service. The cameras also covered the spot where staff change into their emergency gear, so employees were filmed in underwear. IMY accepted that the public-task legal basis (Art. 6(1)(e)) existed, but found breaches of the fairness principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)) and security/organisational measures (Art. 32(1) and 32(4)), since no instructions existed on how the footage could be used. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 350,000, of which SEK 300,000 relates to Art. 5 and SEK 50,000 to Art. 32. The surveillance ended on 6 May 2021.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) fined a controller approximately €2000 (RON 9839) for failing to provide the DPA with requested information during an investigation. Furthermore, the controller received a warning for not fulfilling a data deletion request.

The Garante opened its own investigation into the App IO, the Italian government's access point app run by PagoPA S.p.A. It found that the app sends device and usage data to Google and Mixpanel without the consent required by art. 122 of the Codice, that a deterministic identifier linked to the tax code allows re-identification, and that transfers to non-EU providers lack safeguards. Services from over 5,000 public bodies were also activated by default. The Garante, acting urgently, ordered a temporary limitation of the Google and Mixpanel processing, an order to move to opt-in service activation, and an information request, and reserved any sanctions.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a radio station €2000 (reduced to €1200) for failing to provide a link to its cookie policy in their cookie banner and for installing cookies that are not strictly necessary on user devices without obtaining prior consent.

The Norwegian DPA fined a company approximately €14,700 (NOK 150,000) for taking over an employee's work email account during her notice period without warning her, without giving her the opportunity to delete personal content, and despite her objection, thereby violating Articles 6(1)(f), 13, 17(1)(e), and 21 GDPR.

After a newspaper reported that millions of recorded calls to the 1177 healthcare advice line were openly accessible online, IMY opened supervision of the Region Sörmland board. IMY found that the board collected callers' phone numbers and municipality IDs to route calls to the provider MedHelp AB without giving the information required by Article 13, which also breached the transparency principle in Article 5(1)(a). The processing itself was found lawful and data-minimised. Because the lack of information affected a large number of care seekers, IMY imposed an administrative fine of SEK 250,000.

After a newspaper reported that millions of recorded calls to the 1177 healthcare advice line were openly exposed online, IMY opened supervision of the regional boards using the service, including Region Värmland. IMY found that callers were not informed that their phone number and municipality ID were collected so calls could be routed to the care provider MedHelp AB. Missing were the controller's identity and contact details, purpose, legal basis, access right and the DPO contact. IMY found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 250,000. The data minimisation and legal basis for the processing were found to be fine.

After a newspaper reported that millions of recorded calls to the 1177 healthcare advice line were openly accessible online, IMY opened supervision of the Stockholm health board. It found that the board, as controller, did not inform callers about its collection of their phone number and municipality ID, or about its later collection of call information from the provider MedHelp AB for follow-up and quality purposes. This breached Articles 13 and 14 and the transparency principle in Article 5(1)(a). IMY imposed an administrative fine of SEK 500,000 and ordered the board to provide the information within two months of the decision becoming final. The underlying processing itself was found lawful.

MedHelp AB, the care provider answering calls to the Swedish healthcare advice line 1177, was investigated after a newspaper reported that millions of recorded calls were openly accessible on the internet. IMY found four infringements: disclosing patient data to a Thai company, MediCall, without legal basis; leaving the call recordings on a storage server exposed without protection; not informing callers about the data processing; and not backing up the recordings. IMY imposed a total administrative fine of SEK 12,000,000 and ordered MedHelp to inform callers and to introduce proper backups within two months of the decision becoming final.

A Computer Sweden article in February 2019 revealed that recorded calls to the 1177 healthcare advice line were openly accessible on the internet. IMY found that Voice Integrate Nordic AB was a processor for MedHelp and stored the recordings on its Voice NAS server. The server was exposed to the internet without any protection, because of a misconfiguration, for an unknown period until 18 February 2019. IMY estimated 650,000 to 900,000 calls were affected, containing sensitive health data covered by professional secrecy. IMY held that Voice breached Article 32(1) and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 650,000.
The Spanish DPA ordered a processor (Amazon Web Services) to answer an erasure request from a data subject that had not been completed by the controller (a news website).

The Litigation Chamber of the Belgian DPA ordered the Belgian Special Tax Inspectorate to comply with a complainant's requests to exercise their rights under Articles 14, 15, 16, and 18 GDPR. The Chamber held that subjective information can constitute personal data under the GDPR, and that restrictions to data subject rights in a Belgian income tax law are formulated too broadly and are therefore not applicable.

Moss municipality merged its health-clinic IT system with that of Rygge municipality and converted about 28,000 patient records. The conversion produced many errors: vaccines wrongly registered, wrong pregnancy and substance-use data, and patient data exposed to staff without a need for access with no traceability. The Datatilsynet found that the municipality had done no risk assessment and insufficient testing, and that the conduct was negligent. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 500,000, reduced from the amount first notified after the municipality's response and comparison with similar cases.

The UK DPA fined Solarwave Limited approximately €116,000 (£100,000) for sending direct marketing communications to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service who had not given their prior consent. In calculating this fine, the DPA considered, among other things, that Solawave Limited acted contrary to detailed guidelines it ought to have been aware of, and continued to make unsolicited calls pending the outcome of the ICO's investigation.

The Spanish DPA determined that the Spanish Tax Authority had complied with GDPR requirements when introducing a new biometric system used to register employees' working hours and building access. It further determined that the Authority had given data subjects adequate information about the system.

The Estonian data protection inspectorate issued a binding precept to Viimsi Uudised OÜ, a local news portal, after a person asked for a copy of their personal data under GDPR Article 15 and received no answer. The company ignored the access request and also did not follow the inspectorate's earlier proposal to provide the copy. The inspectorate found that the failure to respond breached the company's duty to answer within one month. It ordered the company to provide the copy by 18 June 2021 and did not impose a fine, but warned of a 2,000 euro penalty payment if the order is not met.

The Spanish DPA fined a company €26,000 (reduced to €19,600) for recording images of their employees' resting room and for not offering up-to-date information about the use of video surveillance at the workplace.

Two former employees complained that their employer, a small company, monitored staff through a video surveillance system inside its offices without informing them. The company said the internal cameras had been switched off since 2008 and that only common-area and perimeter cameras were active, and it answered the Authority's requests only after repeated reminders. The Authority found infringements of the principles of lawfulness/fairness/transparency and purpose limitation and of accountability. It ordered the company to remove the five internal cameras within one month and destroy any material collected, and fined it EUR 15,000.

The Italian DPA imposed a provisional limitation on the processing performed by the Mitiga Italia App, an app used to certify compliance with covid regulations by people wanting to attend sporting events. The limitation is be enforced for as long as necessary for the DPA to establish the legal basis of processing, and to establish whether the data processed was adequately limited.

The UK DPA fined the Conservative Party £10,000 in relation to 1,190,281 direct marketing emails sent as a part of its Brexit campaign. In particular, the DPA held that the Conservative Party had not collected valid consent for the 51 emails sent to the complainants in violation of the PECR, which implements the e-Privacy Directive in the UK.
